title: The Amazing World of Solutes, Solvents, and Solutions
subject: Science
chapter: 9. The Amazing World of Solutes, Solvents, and Solutions
description: Solutes, solvents and solutions, saturation, concentration and solubility (including gases), and density — its formula, units, measurement of mass and volume, and how temperature and pressure change it.

questions.question: Why does every sip of homemade ORS taste the same, no matter how much you drink?
options: Sugar and salt are spread evenly through the water
Sugar and salt settle evenly at the bottom of the glass
Salt dissolves fully but the sugar stays suspended
The tongue cannot sense small changes in sweetness
questions.explanation: ORS is a solution: the sugar and salt are distributed evenly throughout the water, so each sip has the same composition. Settling or suspension would make sips differ.

questions.question: Which of these forms a NON-uniform mixture when stirred into water?
questions.explanation: Chalk powder, sand and sawdust do not spread evenly in water — the components stay visible, so the mixture is non-uniform. Salt, sugar and ORS form uniform mixtures (solutions).

questions.question: Which observation would tell you that a mixture is NON-uniform?
options: Every spoonful of it tastes exactly the same as the others
It looks perfectly clear and even after it is stirred well
Its components can be seen separately, by eye or with a lens
It pours easily from one container into another one
questions.explanation: In non-uniform mixtures the components can be seen separately, either with the naked eye or a magnifying device. Uniform mixtures look even and taste the same throughout.

questions.question: In some non-uniform mixtures, a magnifying device is needed to see the components separately.
questions.explanation: The chapter says components of non-uniform mixtures can be seen either with the naked eye OR with a magnifying device — so some need magnification.

questions.question: A student claims a mixture is a solution ONLY when a solid dissolves in a liquid. Which example proves the claim wrong?
options: Sand stirred into a bucket of water
questions.explanation: Gases such as oxygen dissolve evenly in water, giving a uniform mixture — a solution — with no solid involved. Sand, sawdust and chalk give non-uniform mixtures, not solutions.

questions.question: Sawdust floats on water while sand sinks. Which idea from the chapter explains this difference?
options: How well each dissolves in water
questions.explanation: The chapter leads from this observation into density: whether an object floats or sinks is largely about its density compared with the liquid. Neither sand nor sawdust dissolves, so solubility and saturation are not the point.

questions.question: Select the mixtures that are NON-uniform.
questions.explanation: Sand and sawdust do not spread evenly — their particles stay visible. Salt, sugar and oxygen dissolve to form uniform mixtures (solutions).

questions.question: When chalk powder is mixed with water, the chalk spreads evenly and a solution is formed.
questions.explanation: Chalk powder does NOT distribute evenly in water; the mixture is non-uniform, so it is not a solution.

questions.question: Which statement about solutions is NOT correct?
options: A solution is a uniform mixture of two or more substances
A solution can form when a gas dissolves in a liquid
Its components can be seen separately with a magnifier
A solution can form when two liquids are mixed together
questions.explanation: In a solution the components are NOT visible separately — that is the mark of a non-uniform mixture. The other three statements all match the chapter.

questions.question: The presence of different gases in the atmosphere is an example of a uniform mixture.
questions.explanation: Exercise 1(v) is TRUE: the gases of the atmosphere are mixed evenly, which is what makes a mixture uniform.

questions.question: In a glass of salt water, the salt is the ______.
questions.explanation: When a solid is dissolved in a liquid, the solid is the solute and the liquid is the solvent; together they make the solution.

questions.question: When a solid dissolves in a liquid to form a solution, the liquid component is called the ______.
questions.explanation: The liquid that does the dissolving is the solvent; the dissolved solid is the solute.

questions.question: 20 mL of liquid A is mixed with 80 mL of liquid B and they form a solution. Which is the solvent, and why?
options: A, because it is present in the smaller amount
A, because the smaller liquid dissolves faster
B, because it is present in the larger amount
Neither — two liquids never form a solution
questions.explanation: For two liquids, the one present in the larger amount is the solvent and the smaller one is the solute. Two liquids can certainly form a solution.

questions.question: In the chashni of gulab jamun, a LARGE amount of sugar is dissolved in a SMALL amount of water. What is the solvent?
options: Sugar — it is present in the larger amount
Both — neither substance is clearly in excess
Neither — chashni is a non-uniform mixture
Water — the liquid that does the dissolving
questions.explanation: The 'smaller amount = solute' rule is only for two liquids. Here a solid dissolves in a liquid, so the liquid (water) is the solvent even though there is more sugar.

questions.question: In sugar syrup (chashni), sugar is treated as the solvent because there is more sugar than water.
questions.explanation: Water remains the solvent and sugar the solute: for a solid in a liquid, the liquid is the solvent regardless of amounts.

questions.question: When two liquids form a solution, the one present in the smaller amount is called the solute.
questions.explanation: For liquid–liquid solutions the component present in less quantity is the solute and the other is the solvent.

questions.question: A spoon of baking soda is stirred into 50 mL of water and dissolves. Identify the solute and solvent.
options: Both baking soda and water are solutes
Both baking soda and water are solvents
questions.explanation: The solid that dissolves (baking soda) is the solute; the liquid it dissolves in (water) is the solvent.

questions.question: Why can the rule 'the component in the smaller amount is the solute' NOT be used for chashni?
options: That rule works only when both amounts are exactly equal
Sugar is not a true solute because it melts in syrup
The rule is for two liquids; chashni is a solid in a liquid
Chashni is not a true solution, so no such rule applies
questions.explanation: The smaller-amount rule applies when two liquids are mixed. For a solid dissolved in a liquid, the solid is always the solute, even if there is more of it.

questions.question: Which pairs correctly name the solute and solvent?
options: Salt water — solute: salt; solvent: water
Sugar syrup — solute: water; solvent: sugar
ORS — solutes: sugar and salt; solvent: water
Sand in water — solute: sand; solvent: water
questions.explanation: Salt and the sugar+salt of ORS are dissolved solids (solutes) in water (solvent). In syrup the solvent is still water. Sand does not dissolve, so it is not a solute at all.

questions.question: Fig. 9.3 is a magnified picture of a solution. How are the solute particles arranged in it?
options: Collected at the bottom of the solvent
Floating as a layer on top of the solvent
Clumped together at the sides of the container
questions.explanation: The figure shows solute evenly distributed in the solvent — this even spread is what makes a solution uniform.

questions.question: In Activity 9.1, salt eventually stops dissolving and settles at the bottom. The solution is now ______ at that temperature.
questions.explanation: When added solute stops dissolving and settles, the solvent has reached its limit — the solution is saturated at that temperature.

questions.question: Which description matches an UNSATURATED solution?
options: No more solute can dissolve in it at that temperature
Undissolved solute has settled at its bottom
More solute can still dissolve in it at that temperature
It contains the maximum possible amount of solute
questions.explanation: An unsaturated solution can dissolve more solute at the given temperature; the other three describe a saturated solution.

questions.question: Which ONE of these statements is the most appropriate?
options: A saturated solution can still dissolve more solute at a given temperature
An unsaturated solution holds the maximum solute possible at a given temperature
A saturated solution forms only when the temperature is high
No more solute can dissolve in a saturated solution at that temperature
questions.explanation: Exercise 5: statement (iii) is correct. (i) and (ii) swap the meanings of saturated and unsaturated, and (iv) is wrong because saturation can occur at any temperature.

questions.question: Why is the statement 'A saturated solution forms only at high temperatures' NOT appropriate?
options: Saturation happens at any temperature once the solute limit is reached
Saturated solutions actually form only at low temperatures
Temperature has no effect on how much solute can dissolve
High temperatures stop any solution from becoming saturated
questions.explanation: A solution is saturated when the solvent can hold no more solute AT THAT temperature — this can happen at 20 °C just as at 70 °C. Temperature does change the limit, but does not restrict saturation to hot solutions.

questions.question: An unsaturated solution has more solute dissolved than a saturated solution at the same temperature.
questions.explanation: Exercise 1(iv) is FALSE. The saturated solution holds the maximum solute; an unsaturated one holds less and can still dissolve more.

questions.question: Glucose has completely dissolved in water and no more glucose can dissolve at that temperature. This is a ______ solution of glucose.
questions.explanation: Exercise 2(iv): when no more solute can dissolve at a given temperature, the solution is saturated.

questions.question: A saturated salt solution at 20 °C has some undissolved salt at the bottom. It is heated to 50 °C with stirring. Predict what happens.
options: More salt settles out, making the solution more saturated
Nothing changes because saturation does not depend on temperature
The undissolved salt dissolves; the solution is now unsaturated
The salt floats upwards as the warm water becomes less dense
questions.explanation: For most solids, solubility rises with temperature, so the saturated solution behaves as unsaturated when heated and the extra salt dissolves — exactly what happened with baking soda in Activity 9.2.

questions.question: Why must the word 'saturated' always be linked to a particular temperature?
options: Saturated solutions exist only at room temperature
Changing temperature changes the amount of solvent present
Solutes turn into solvents when a solution is heated
The amount of solute a solvent can hold changes with temperature
questions.explanation: Solubility depends on temperature, so a solution that is saturated at 20 °C may be unsaturated at 50 °C. The temperature must therefore be stated.

questions.question: A solution that is saturated at one temperature behaves as an unsaturated solution if its temperature is increased.
questions.explanation: Because solubility of most solids increases with temperature, raising the temperature lets the same solution dissolve more solute — it behaves as unsaturated.

questions.question: In Activity 9.1 (adding salt spoon by spoon to half a tumbler of water), which quantity is deliberately changed by the student?
options: The volume of water in the glass tumbler
The total amount of salt added to the water
The temperature of the water in the tumbler
The size of the spoon used for adding salt
questions.explanation: The water volume, temperature and spoon stay fixed; the student keeps adding salt (the changed variable) and observes whether it dissolves (the observed result).

questions.question: Select the statements that are true of a SATURATED solution.
options: No more solute dissolves in it at that temperature
Added solute settles undissolved at the bottom
It always contains very little solute
It can never be made unsaturated again
questions.explanation: Saturation means the solvent holds its maximum solute at that temperature, so extra solute settles. The dissolved part is still a uniform solution, it may hold a lot of solute, and heating can make it unsaturated.

questions.question: What does the chapter call the amount of solute present in a fixed quantity of solution (or solvent)?
questions.explanation: Concentration is the amount of solute in a fixed quantity of solution or solvent. Solubility is the MAXIMUM that can dissolve; density is mass per unit volume.

questions.question: Which solution is more concentrated: 2 spoons of salt in 100 mL of water, or 4 spoons of salt in 50 mL of water?
options: 2 spoons of salt in 100 mL of water
Both have exactly the same concentration
It cannot be decided without the temperature
4 spoons of salt in 50 mL of water
questions.explanation: Concentration compares solute per fixed amount of solvent: 4 spoons per 50 mL is 8 spoons per 100 mL, four times the 2 spoons per 100 mL of the first solution.

questions.question: 4 spoons of salt in 50 mL of water is how many times as concentrated as 2 spoons of salt in 100 mL of water?
questions.explanation: Per 100 mL: the first has 4 × 2 = 8 spoons, the second has 2 spoons. 8 ÷ 2 = 4, so it is four times as concentrated — not just twice, even though it has twice the salt, because it also has half the water.

questions.question: 'Dilute' and 'concentrated' are relative terms — a solution is dilute or concentrated only in comparison with another.
questions.explanation: The chapter states that dilute and concentrated are relative terms; the 1-spoon solution is dilute compared with the 2-spoon solution.

questions.question: Which statement about concentration is NOT correct?
options: Concentration is the amount of solute in a fixed quantity of solution
A solution with less solute in a fixed quantity is called dilute
A concentrated solution always has more solvent than a dilute one
The same solution can be dilute next to one and concentrated next to another
questions.explanation: Concentration is about the SOLUTE in a fixed amount of solution — a concentrated solution has more solute, not more solvent. The other statements follow the chapter.

questions.question: 3 spoons of salt are dissolved in 150 mL of water, and 1 spoon in 50 mL of water. Compare their concentrations.
options: The 150 mL solution is more concentrated
The 50 mL solution is more concentrated
The 150 mL solution is three times as strong
questions.explanation: Both have 1 spoon per 50 mL (3 ÷ 150 = 1 ÷ 50), so the concentrations are equal even though the amounts differ.

questions.question: Which word describes a solution with a SMALL amount of solute in a fixed quantity of solution?
questions.explanation: A solution with less solute is dilute; one with more solute is concentrated. 'Saturated' and 'dense' mean different things.

questions.question: Which changes would make a salt solution MORE concentrated?
options: Dissolving more salt in the same water
Boiling away some of the water
Pouring half of it into another glass
Stirring it for a longer time
questions.explanation: Concentration = solute per fixed quantity of solvent, so adding solute or removing solvent (as when salt water is boiled at Ningel) raises it. Adding water lowers it; pouring some away or stirring changes neither solute nor solvent proportion.

questions.question: Pouring half of a sugar solution into another glass makes the half left behind more concentrated.
questions.explanation: Both halves have the same proportion of sugar to water as the original — concentration is about the amount of solute in a FIXED quantity, not the total amount.

questions.question: What is 'solubility' as defined in the chapter?
options: The amount of solute actually present in a fixed quantity of solution
The maximum amount of solute that dissolves in a fixed quantity of solvent
The speed at which a solute disappears when stirred into a solvent
The temperature at which a solute begins to dissolve in a solvent
questions.explanation: Solubility is the MAXIMUM solute a fixed quantity of solvent can dissolve at a particular temperature. The amount actually present is the concentration.

questions.question: In the chapter summary, solubility is stated for what fixed quantity of solvent?
questions.explanation: The Snapshots define solubility as the maximum solute dissolved in a fixed quantity (100 mL) of solution or solvent at a particular temperature.

questions.question: In Activity 9.2, undissolved baking soda dissolved when the water was warmed from 20 °C to 50 °C, and again from 50 °C to 70 °C. What is the correct inference?
options: Baking soda dissolves equally well at all three temperatures
Heating turned the baking soda into a gas that escaped
Water at 20 °C dissolves the most baking soda of the three
Water at 70 °C dissolves more baking soda than water at 50 °C
questions.explanation: Each time the temperature rose, more baking soda could dissolve, so solubility increased with temperature: 70 °C > 50 °C > 20 °C.

questions.question: A saturated baking soda solution made at 70 °C is left to cool back to 20 °C. Predict what will most likely happen.
options: Some baking soda separates out as its solubility falls
More baking soda dissolves as the cooler water gets denser
Nothing happens because a saturated solution stays saturated
The baking soda changes into a gas and bubbles away
questions.explanation: Water at 20 °C can hold less baking soda than water at 70 °C. The solution now contains more solute than 20 °C water can dissolve, so the excess comes out of solution.

questions.question: In Activity 9.2, which quantity is the one being OBSERVED (the result), rather than the one being changed?
options: The temperature of the water in the beaker
The amount of baking soda that dissolves
The volume of water taken in the beaker
The number of times the glass rod is stirred
questions.explanation: The experimenter changes the temperature (20 → 50 → 70 °C) and watches how much baking soda dissolves. Water volume (about 50 mL) is kept fixed.

questions.question: What is kept the SAME throughout Activity 9.2 so that the comparison is fair?
options: The total amount of baking soda added
The amount of baking soda left undissolved
questions.explanation: Only the temperature is changed on purpose; the same ~50 mL of water is used so that any extra dissolving must be due to temperature, not more solvent.

questions.question: For most substances, solubility increases as the temperature increases.
questions.explanation: The chapter states that for most substances solubility increases with an increase in temperature.

questions.question: In Activity 9.2, the water at 20 °C dissolved the most baking soda of the three temperatures tested.
questions.explanation: The amount dissolved at 20 °C was the LEAST; water at 70 °C dissolved the most.

questions.question: What is the chemical name of baking soda, the solute used in Activity 9.2?
questions.explanation: The activity names baking soda as sodium hydrogen carbonate. Sodium chloride is common salt and calcium carbonate is chalk.

questions.question: In the Fig. 9.7 setup, which items are part of HEATING or SUPPORTING the beaker (rather than measuring or stirring)?
questions.explanation: The spirit lamp supplies heat and the tripod with wire gauze supports the beaker above the flame. The thermometer measures and the glass rod stirs.

questions.question: Two students each dissolve as much salt as 50 mL of water will take — one at 20 °C, the other at 60 °C. Which statement is correct?
options: Both hold the same salt because both are saturated
The 20 °C solution holds more because cold water is denser
The 60 °C solution most likely holds more dissolved salt
Neither can be saturated because 50 mL is too little water
questions.explanation: Both are saturated, but saturation is temperature-dependent: warmer water usually dissolves more solid, so the 60 °C solution contains more salt. 'Saturated' does not mean 'same amount'.

questions.question: Suppose a student records: 20 °C → 4 spoons of a solid dissolve; 40 °C → 6 spoons; 60 °C → 9 spoons (same water). What does the data show?
options: Solubility of the solid falls with temperature
Temperature has no effect on the solid's solubility
The solid behaves like a gas dissolving in water
Solubility of the solid rises with temperature
questions.explanation: More spoons dissolve at each higher temperature, so solubility increases with temperature — the pattern the chapter says most solids follow (unlike gases).

questions.question: What sustains fish, aquatic plants and other organisms living in water?
options: Sand settled on the river bed
questions.explanation: Even though it is present in small amounts, dissolved oxygen sustains all aquatic life.

questions.question: To what extent does oxygen dissolve in water?
questions.explanation: Oxygen dissolves in water only to a small extent, yet this small quantity is enough to keep aquatic life alive.

questions.question: How does the solubility of gases in liquids generally change as temperature rises?
questions.explanation: Unlike most solids, gases become LESS soluble as the liquid warms — more oxygen dissolves in cold water than in warm water.

questions.question: Oxygen gas is more soluble in hot water than in cold water.
questions.explanation: Exercise 1(i) is FALSE. Gas solubility decreases with temperature, so oxygen is more soluble in COLD water.

questions.question: Which is the CORRECTED version of the false statement 'Oxygen gas is more soluble in hot water than in cold water'?
options: Oxygen gas is equally soluble in hot and cold water
Oxygen gas does not dissolve in water at any temperature
Oxygen gas is more soluble in hot water than salt is
Oxygen gas is more soluble in cold water than in hot water
questions.explanation: The chapter says more oxygen can dissolve in cold water and solubility of oxygen decreases as water warms.

questions.question: A beaker of water containing dissolved baking soda AND dissolved oxygen is warmed. How are the two solutes affected?
options: More baking soda can dissolve, but less oxygen stays dissolved
Both dissolve more, since heat speeds up dissolving
Both dissolve less, since heat drives everything out
Less baking soda dissolves, but more oxygen dissolves
questions.explanation: Solubility of most solids (baking soda) increases with temperature, while solubility of gases (oxygen) decreases — the two trends are opposite.

questions.question: In summer a shallow pond warms up considerably. Predict the effect on the fish.
options: More oxygen dissolves, so fish become more active
Less oxygen stays dissolved, so fish may struggle
Oxygen solubility is unchanged, so fish are unaffected
Oxygen spreads more evenly, so fish breathe more easily
questions.explanation: Warm water holds less dissolved oxygen (gas solubility falls with temperature), so there is less oxygen available for aquatic life.

questions.question: A mixture of gases dissolved in water is a uniform mixture.
questions.explanation: Gases dissolve evenly in water, so the mixture is uniform — a solution.

questions.question: Select the statements about gases in water that are correct.
options: Many gases, including oxygen, dissolve in water
Gas solubility generally decreases as temperature rises
Gas solubility increases strongly on heating
Dissolved gases form a non-uniform mixture
questions.explanation: Gases such as oxygen do dissolve (a little) and evenly; their solubility falls with rising temperature, the opposite of most solids.

questions.question: Suppose a student measures dissolved oxygen in the same river water at 10 °C, 20 °C and 30 °C and gets steadily smaller values. Which chapter idea does this match?
options: Gas solubility decreases as temperature increases
Solid solubility increases as temperature increases
Density of water decreases as temperature increases
questions.explanation: Falling dissolved oxygen with rising temperature is exactly the chapter's statement that the solubility of gases generally decreases as temperature increases.

questions.topic: Floating, Sinking and the Idea of Density
questions.question: While washing rice, husk floats on the water and rice sinks. Why?
options: Husk is denser than water; rice is less dense
Husk is less dense than water; rice is denser
Husk dissolves slightly while rice does not
Rice absorbs water while husk repels it
questions.explanation: Objects that float are generally less dense than the liquid, while those that sink are denser — husk is light for its size, rice is heavier for its size.

questions.topic: Floating, Sinking and the Idea of Density
questions.question: You pour oil into a glass containing water and the oil floats on top. What does this tell you?
options: Oil and water have the same density
questions.explanation: Exercise 3: the less dense liquid floats on the denser one, so water is denser than oil. If oil dissolved, it would not form a separate layer.

questions.topic: Floating, Sinking and the Idea of Density
questions.question: An unpeeled orange floats in water but the same orange sinks after peeling (Fig. 9.25). What best explains this?
options: Peeling removes the oil that makes the orange float
The peeled orange absorbs water and becomes heavier
The peel dissolves a little, making the water denser
Air in the peel lowers the whole orange's average density
questions.explanation: The peel is light and air-filled, so with the peel the orange's mass per unit volume is less than water's and it floats. Without the peel, the dense fruit alone is denser than water and sinks.

questions.topic: Floating, Sinking and the Idea of Density
questions.question: According to the chapter's 'Note', what is the relationship between density and floating?
options: Density matters, but it is not the only deciding factor
Density alone fully decides whether anything floats
Only the shape of an object decides whether it floats
Only the mass of an object decides whether it floats
questions.explanation: The Note says the density of a substance is NOT the only factor that decides whether it floats or sinks — density explains it only partially.

questions.topic: Floating, Sinking and the Idea of Density
questions.question: The chapter states that density is the only factor deciding whether an object floats or sinks in a liquid.
questions.explanation: The chapter's Note explicitly says density is NOT the only factor; it explains floating and sinking only partially.

questions.topic: Floating, Sinking and the Idea of Density
questions.question: A wooden stick and an iron rod are the same size, yet the iron rod feels much heavier. Which property explains this?
options: Iron has a larger volume than wood
Iron has a higher density than wood
Iron has a smaller mass than wood
Iron absorbs more water than wood
questions.explanation: Same size means same volume; iron has more mass in that volume, i.e. a higher density — the 'heaviness' property the chapter introduces.

questions.topic: Floating, Sinking and the Idea of Density
questions.question: A raw egg sinks in a tumbler of tap water. Which single change to the WATER would make the egg float?
options: Warm it gently so that it becomes less dense
Use much more tap water in a much bigger tumbler
Dissolve plenty of salt in it to raise its density
Stir it quickly to spread the water evenly
questions.explanation: The egg floats only if the liquid becomes denser than the egg. Dissolving a lot of salt increases the water's density; warming would lower it, and more water or stirring does not change density.

questions.topic: Floating, Sinking and the Idea of Density
questions.question: Why was bamboo chosen in ancient times for making rafts?
options: It is heavy and solid, so it stays steady
It dissolves slowly, so it lasts in water
It is dense, so it sits low in the water
It is light and hollow, so it floats easily
questions.explanation: The 'Ever heard of' box says bamboo is light, hollow, and floats easily on water — ideal for rafts.

questions.topic: Floating, Sinking and the Idea of Density
questions.question: Which of these are described in the chapter as FLOATING on water?
questions.explanation: Oil floats on water and husk floats while washing rice. Sand sinks, and the peeled orange sinks in exercise 8.

questions.topic: Floating, Sinking and the Idea of Density
questions.question: The Dead Sea is extremely salty. Based on the chapter, why might this make it easy for a person to float there?
options: Dissolved salt makes the water much lighter than normal water
Dissolved salt makes the water much denser than normal water
Salt removes the oxygen that would otherwise pull swimmers down
Salt lowers the water temperature, making it support more weight
questions.explanation: Just as salt makes tap water dense enough to float an egg, the Dead Sea's huge salt content makes its water far denser than a human body, so people float easily.

questions.question: How does the chapter define density?
options: The volume occupied by a unit mass of a substance
The total mass of an object regardless of its size
The mass present in a unit volume of a substance
The space an object occupies when fully immersed
questions.explanation: Density = mass per unit volume. The second option is inverted, and the others describe mass and volume respectively.

questions.question: Which formula gives density?
questions.explanation: Density = Mass/Volume. Dividing the other way or multiplying gives something else entirely.

questions.question: What is the SI unit of density?
questions.explanation: SI units of mass and volume are kg and m³, so the SI unit of density is kilogram per cubic metre (kg/m³). g/mL and g/cm³ are convenient non-SI units.

questions.question: According to the chapter's conversion, 1 kg/m³ is equal to ______.
questions.explanation: 1 kg/m³ = 1000 g / 1000 L = 1 g/L — a kilogram is 1000 g and a cubic metre is 1000 L.

questions.question: Using the chapter's conversion factor, 1 kg/m³ equals how many g/cm³?
questions.explanation: 1 kg/m³ = 1 g/1000 cm³ = 0.001 g/cm³. A value in kg/m³ is 1000 times the value in g/cm³ (water: 1000 kg/m³ ≈ 1 g/cm³).

questions.question: Does the density of a substance depend on its shape or size?
options: No — it is independent of shape and size
Yes — larger pieces always have higher density
Yes — flatter pieces always have lower density
Only the size matters, not the shape
questions.explanation: Density is a property of the substance, independent of shape or size; it depends on temperature and pressure instead.

questions.question: Which factors does the chapter say the density of a substance DEPENDS on?
questions.explanation: Density is independent of shape and size but dependent on temperature and pressure.

questions.question: Pressure mainly affects the density of which state of matter?
questions.explanation: Pressure primarily affects the density of gases; its effect on solids and liquids is negligible.

questions.question: A packet of oil is labelled 1 litre but weighs only 910 g. What does this tell you about the oil's density?
questions.explanation: 910 g ÷ 1000 mL = 0.91 g/mL, below water's roughly 1 g/mL. That is why oil floats on water.

questions.question: Which statement about density is NOT correct?
options: The density of a gas is hardly changed by pressure
The density of a substance does not depend on its shape
The density of a substance depends on its temperature
The density of a solid is hardly changed by pressure
questions.explanation: Pressure PRIMARILY affects gases — compressing a gas raises its density a lot. Solids and liquids are barely affected. The other statements match the chapter.

questions.question: The mass of 1 mL of water is close to 1 g at room temperature.
questions.explanation: The chapter says 1 mL of water has a mass close to 1 g, so 100 mL of water is about 100 g.

questions.question: The SI unit of density is gram per millilitre (g/mL).
questions.explanation: The SI unit is kg/m³. g/mL is a convenient unit used for liquids, not the SI unit.

questions.question: An aluminium block has a mass of 27 g and a volume of 10 cm³. What is its density?
questions.explanation: Density = 27 g ÷ 10 cm³ = 2.7 g/cm³.

questions.question: The relative density of aluminium with respect to water is 2.7. What kind of quantity is this?
questions.explanation: Relative density is a ratio of two densities, so the units cancel and it is a pure number.

questions.question: How is the relative density of a substance with respect to water calculated?
options: Density of the substance ÷ density of water at that temperature
Density of water ÷ density of the substance at that temperature
Density of the substance × density of water at that temperature
Density of the substance − density of water at that temperature
questions.explanation: Relative density = density of the substance / density of water (at the same temperature).

questions.question: 'Aluminium has a relative density of 2.7' means that ______.
options: 1 cm³ of aluminium has a mass of 2.7 kg
aluminium is 2.7 times as dense as water
aluminium is 2.7 g/cm³ heavier than water
water is 2.7 times as dense as aluminium
questions.explanation: Relative density compares with water: aluminium's density (2.7 g/cm³) is 2.7 times water's (about 1 g/cm³). 1 cm³ of aluminium is 2.7 g, not kg.

questions.question: A stone sculpture weighs 225 g and has a volume of 90 cm³. What is its density, and will it float or sink in water?
questions.explanation: Exercise 4: 225 ÷ 90 = 2.5 g/cm³, more than water's ~1 g/cm³, so the sculpture sinks.

questions.question: An object has a mass of 400 g and a volume of 40 cm³. What is its density?
questions.explanation: Exercise 7: density = 400 g ÷ 40 cm³ = 10 g/cm³.

questions.question: Object A: mass 200 g, volume 40 cm³. Object B: mass 240 g, volume 60 cm³. Which is denser?
options: Object B, because it has the larger mass
Both — each has a density of 4.5 g/cm³
questions.explanation: Exercise 9: A = 200 ÷ 40 = 5 g/cm³; B = 240 ÷ 60 = 4 g/cm³. A is denser even though B has more mass.

questions.question: Reema moulds 120 g of clay into a cube of volume 60 cm³, then flattens it into a thin sheet. What happens to its density?
options: Decreases, because the sheet is much thinner
Stays 2 g/cm³ — mass and volume are unchanged
Increases, because the sheet is more compact
Becomes zero, because the sheet is flat
questions.explanation: Exercise 10: density = 120 ÷ 60 = 2 g/cm³. Reshaping changes neither mass nor volume, and density is independent of shape, so it stays 2 g/cm³.

questions.question: A block of iron has a mass of 600 g and a density of 7.9 g/cm³. What is its volume?
questions.explanation: Exercise 11: volume = mass ÷ density = 600 ÷ 7.9 ≈ 75.9 cm³, about 76 cm³. 4740 comes from multiplying instead of dividing.

questions.question: In the chapter's worked example, a stone of mass 16.400 g displaces 5 mL of water. What is its density?
questions.explanation: Volume = 5 mL = 5 cm³; density = 16.400 ÷ 5 = 3.28 g/cm³, as calculated on page 146.

questions.question: Compare 10 cm³ of aluminium (density 2.7 g/cm³) with 10 cm³ of water. Which is correct?
options: Both have the same mass, 10 g
questions.explanation: 10 cm³ of aluminium = 27 g; 10 cm³ of water ≈ 10 g. The difference is 27 − 10 = 17 g.

questions.question: Relative density has no units because it is a ratio of two densities.
questions.explanation: Dividing a density by the density of water cancels the units, leaving a pure number such as 2.7 for aluminium.

questions.question: An object with a density of 0.8 g/cm³ will sink in water.
questions.explanation: 0.8 g/cm³ is LESS than water's ~1 g/cm³, so the object floats.

questions.topic: Measuring Mass: Balances, Mass and Weight
questions.question: Which instrument is used to measure the mass of an object?
questions.explanation: Mass is measured with a balance (for example a digital weighing balance); a measuring cylinder measures volume.

questions.topic: Measuring Mass: Balances, Mass and Weight
questions.question: What is 'mass' according to the chapter?
options: The quantity of matter present in an object
The amount of space occupied by an object
The force with which Earth pulls an object
The heaviness of an object per unit volume
questions.explanation: Mass is the quantity of matter in an object. Space occupied is volume, Earth's pull is weight, and heaviness per unit volume is density.

questions.topic: Measuring Mass: Balances, Mass and Weight
questions.question: In Activity 9.3, why is the tare (reset) button pressed AFTER placing the watch glass on the pan?
options: So the balance can switch from grams to kilograms
So the display reads zero, ignoring the watch glass's mass
So the watch glass is weighed together with the stone
So the balance measures weight rather than the mass
questions.explanation: Taring sets the reading to zero with the watch glass in place, so the next reading shows only the mass of the stone.

questions.topic: Measuring Mass: Balances, Mass and Weight
questions.question: In science, weight is measured in which unit?
questions.explanation: Weight is a force — Earth's pull on an object — and is measured in newtons. Grams and kilograms are units of mass; litres measure volume.

questions.topic: Measuring Mass: Balances, Mass and Weight
questions.question: Most balances actually measure weight but are marked in mass units. Which type of balance is the exception mentioned in the chapter?
questions.explanation: The 'A step further' box says most balances — except two-pan balances like Fig. 9.13 — measure weight but display mass units.

questions.topic: Measuring Mass: Balances, Mass and Weight
questions.question: Weight is the force with which the Earth attracts an object towards itself.
questions.explanation: This is the chapter's definition of weight, measured in newtons (N).

questions.topic: Measuring Mass: Balances, Mass and Weight
questions.question: Mass is measured in newtons, while weight is measured in kilograms.
questions.explanation: It is the other way round: mass is in grams/kilograms and weight (a force) is in newtons.

questions.topic: Measuring Mass: Balances, Mass and Weight
questions.question: How can the mass of a liquid be measured with the digital balance set-up of Activity 9.3?
options: Pour the liquid directly onto the pan of the balance
Replace the watch glass with a beaker and pour the liquid in
Measure its volume in a cylinder and read that as mass
Place the liquid's container on a two-pan balance only
questions.explanation: The Note says to replace the watch glass with a beaker (tare it) and pour in the desired amount of liquid.

questions.topic: Measuring Mass: Balances, Mass and Weight
questions.question: Select the statements about mass and weight that are correct.
options: Mass is the quantity of matter in an object
Mass and weight mean exactly the same in science
Weight is the quantity of matter in an object
questions.explanation: Mass = quantity of matter (g, kg); weight = Earth's pull (N). They are used interchangeably in everyday speech but differ in science.

questions.topic: Measuring Mass: Balances, Mass and Weight
questions.question: Why can a balance that really measures weight still display a useful value in grams?
options: It counts the number of particles in the object
Mass and weight are identical quantities
The gram is the SI unit of force (weight)
On Earth, weight and mass are closely related
questions.explanation: Because weight and mass are closely related on Earth, the scale can be marked in mass units even though the balance senses weight.

questions.topic: Measuring Mass: Balances, Mass and Weight
questions.question: Put these Activity 9.3 steps in order: (P) place the stone on the watch glass, (Q) tare with the watch glass on the pan, (R) switch on and check for zero, (S) note the stone's mass.
questions.explanation: Switch on and check zero, place and tare the watch glass, then place the stone and read its mass.

questions.topic: Volume Units and the Measuring Cylinder
questions.question: What is the SI unit of volume?
questions.explanation: The SI unit of volume is the cubic metre — the volume of a cube with 1 m sides. Litres and cm³ are convenient smaller units.

questions.topic: Volume Units and the Measuring Cylinder
questions.question: One litre (L) is equivalent to ______.
questions.explanation: The chapter says a litre is equivalent to 1 cubic decimetre (dm³); a millilitre equals 1 cm³.

questions.topic: Volume Units and the Measuring Cylinder
questions.question: One millilitre (mL) equals ______, which is also written as 1 cc.
questions.explanation: 1 mL = 1 cm³, and one centimetre cube is also written as one cc.

questions.topic: Volume Units and the Measuring Cylinder
questions.question: A tetra pack says it contains 200 mL of buttermilk. What does this volume equal in cm³?
questions.explanation: Since 1 mL = 1 cm³, 200 mL is 200 cm³.

questions.topic: Volume Units and the Measuring Cylinder
questions.question: Which apparatus does the chapter describe for measuring the volume of liquids?
questions.explanation: A measuring cylinder is a narrow, transparent cylinder with volume markings, used to measure liquid volume.

questions.topic: Volume Units and the Measuring Cylinder
questions.question: Which measuring-cylinder capacities are listed in the chapter?
questions.explanation: The listed sizes are 5, 10, 25, 50, 100 and 250 mL (500 mL is mentioned later). 75 mL and 2 L are not listed.

questions.topic: Volume Units and the Measuring Cylinder
questions.question: One litre is equal to one cubic centimetre.
questions.explanation: One litre equals 1 dm³ (1000 cm³); it is one MILLILITRE that equals 1 cm³.

questions.topic: Volume Units and the Measuring Cylinder
questions.question: How many millilitres are there in 1 dm³?
questions.explanation: 1 dm³ = 1 L, and 1 L = 1000 mL (each mL being 1 cm³).

questions.question: A 100 mL measuring cylinder has 10 small divisions between the 10 mL and 20 mL marks. What is the smallest volume it can read?
questions.explanation: The gap between the big marks is 10 mL and there are 10 divisions, so one division = 10 ÷ 10 = 1 mL.

questions.question: What is the smallest volume a 250 mL measuring cylinder usually reads?
questions.explanation: The chapter gives: 0.1 mL for 10 or 25 mL cylinders, 1 mL for 100 mL, 2 mL for 250 mL and 5 mL for 500 mL.

questions.question: Which measuring cylinder usually reads to the smallest division, 0.1 mL?
questions.explanation: Smaller cylinders are finer: 10 mL and 25 mL cylinders read 0.1 mL, while 500 mL cylinders read only 5 mL.

questions.question: You need exactly 70 mL of water. Which measuring cylinder is the BEST choice, and why?
options: 100 mL — measures it in one step with 1 mL accuracy
50 mL — the smaller the cylinder, the more accurate
500 mL — it holds 70 mL with plenty of room to spare
250 mL — it is the standard size for school laboratories
questions.explanation: A 50 mL cylinder would need two steps (50 + 20), while 250 or 500 mL cylinders are less accurate (2 or 5 mL divisions). The 100 mL cylinder does it in one step at 1 mL accuracy.

questions.question: Why is a 50 mL measuring cylinder NOT convenient for measuring 70 mL of water?
options: Its smallest division of 5 mL makes it inaccurate
70 mL must be measured in two steps (50 mL, then 20 mL)
It is too wide for the water to form a meniscus
It cannot be read because its marks are too close
questions.explanation: The chapter says you would first measure 50 mL and then 20 mL; measuring in more than one step is not convenient.

questions.question: Why does the chapter reject a 500 mL cylinder for measuring 70 mL, even though it can hold it in one step?
options: It cannot be placed on a flat surface safely
Its volume markings begin only at the 100 mL level
Its smallest division is 5 mL, so accuracy is reduced
Water does not form a meniscus in large cylinders
questions.explanation: Large cylinders have coarser divisions (5 mL for 500 mL) than a 100 mL cylinder (1 mL), so the reading is less accurate.

questions.question: What is the curved surface of water inside a measuring cylinder called?
questions.explanation: The curved surface a liquid forms in the cylinder is called the meniscus.

questions.question: For water or any colourless liquid, which part of the meniscus should coincide with the mark being read?
questions.explanation: For water and other colourless liquids, read the mark at the BOTTOM of the meniscus; for coloured liquids, use the top.

questions.question: A student measures 50 mL of a dark coloured syrup in a measuring cylinder. Where should the 50 mL mark coincide?
options: With the bottom of the meniscus
With the top of the meniscus
With the centre of the meniscus
With the surface edge touching glass
questions.explanation: The chapter notes that for coloured liquids the mark should coincide with the TOP of the meniscus — the opposite of the rule for water.

questions.question: When reading a measuring cylinder, where should your eyes be?
options: Well above the cylinder, looking down
Level with the bottom of the meniscus
At the top rim of the measuring cylinder
questions.explanation: Keep the eyes at the level of the bottom of the meniscus (as in Fig. 9.18) to read the volume correctly.

questions.question: Why are measuring cylinders made tall and narrow rather than wide and short like a beaker?
options: A wide container would let the water evaporate away far too quickly
In a narrow column the marks are spread out, so it reads finer volumes
A tall shape is needed so that the liquid can form a proper meniscus
Narrow glass is stronger and does not crack when it is heated
questions.explanation: The chapter's data show narrower, smaller cylinders read finer divisions (0.1 mL for 10 mL vs 5 mL for 500 mL): in a narrow column the same volume rises higher, so the markings are farther apart and more accurate to read.

questions.question: Measuring a required volume in more than one step is considered convenient and preferred.
questions.explanation: The chapter says measuring volume in more than one step is NOT convenient — pick a cylinder that measures it in one step.

questions.question: Which statements about reading a measuring cylinder are correct?
options: Read colourless liquids at the bottom of the meniscus
Read coloured liquids at the top of the meniscus
Keep your eyes well above the liquid level
Read all liquids at the top of the meniscus
A 500 mL cylinder is more accurate than a 100 mL one
questions.explanation: Bottom of meniscus for colourless, top for coloured, eyes level with the meniscus. Larger cylinders have coarser divisions, so they are less accurate.

questions.topic: Volume of Regular and Irregular Solids
questions.question: How is the volume of a cuboid such as a shoe box calculated?
questions.explanation: Volume = l × w × h for cuboid shapes like a notebook, shoe box or dice.

questions.topic: Volume of Regular and Irregular Solids
questions.question: A notebook is 25 cm long, 18 cm wide and 2 cm high. What is its volume?
questions.explanation: Volume = 25 × 18 × 2 = 900 cm³, as in Activity 9.6.

questions.topic: Volume of Regular and Irregular Solids
questions.question: A dice has sides of 2 cm each. What is its volume?
questions.explanation: Volume = 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 cm³. Adding the sides (6) or doubling (4) is a common slip.

questions.topic: Volume of Regular and Irregular Solids
questions.question: A stone lowered into a measuring cylinder raises the water level from 50 mL to 55 mL. What is the stone's volume?
questions.explanation: Volume of the stone = final − initial = 55 − 50 = 5 mL = 5 cm³ (Table 9.2).

questions.topic: Volume of Regular and Irregular Solids
questions.question: Fill in the blanks: the volume of a solid can be measured by displacement, where the solid is ______ in water and the ______ in water level is measured.
questions.explanation: Exercise 2(i): the solid is immersed (put fully under water) and the RISE in the water level equals its volume.

questions.topic: Volume of Regular and Irregular Solids
questions.question: Could the displacement method of Activity 9.7 be used to find the volume of a sugar cube? Why?
options: Yes — any solid object displaces exactly its own volume
No — sugar is too light to push the water level up
Yes — dissolved sugar still raises the level by its volume
No — the sugar would dissolve, so no proper level rise is read
questions.explanation: The method relies on the solid staying intact under water. Sugar dissolves in water (it is a solute), so the water level would not give a reliable measure of the cube's volume.

questions.topic: Volume of Regular and Irregular Solids
questions.question: For the displacement method as described in the chapter to give the object's full volume, the object must be ______.
options: lighter than the water it displaces
questions.explanation: The water rises by the volume of object that is UNDER the surface; the stone and keys in Activity 9.7 sink fully, so the rise equals their whole volume.

questions.topic: Volume of Regular and Irregular Solids
questions.question: Initial water level 50 mL, final level 62 mL after adding a metal piece of mass 30 g. What is the metal's density?
questions.explanation: Volume = 62 − 50 = 12 cm³; density = 30 ÷ 12 = 2.5 g/cm³.

questions.topic: Volume of Regular and Irregular Solids
questions.question: A metal key of mass 24 g raises the water level from 40 mL to 43 mL. What is its density?
questions.explanation: Volume displaced = 43 − 40 = 3 cm³; density = 24 ÷ 3 = 8 g/cm³. 72 comes from multiplying, 0.125 from dividing the wrong way.

questions.topic: Volume of Regular and Irregular Solids
questions.question: For solids, a volume measured as 5 mL in a measuring cylinder can be written as 5 cm³.
questions.explanation: Since 1 mL = 1 cm³, 5 mL of displaced water equals a solid volume of 5 cm³.

questions.topic: Volume of Regular and Irregular Solids
questions.question: The volume of an irregular stone can be found by multiplying its length, width and height.
questions.explanation: l × w × h works only for regular cuboids. An irregular stone's volume is found by water displacement.

questions.topic: Volume of Regular and Irregular Solids
questions.question: For which objects can the volume be found directly using l × w × h?
questions.explanation: A shoe box and a dice are cuboid shapes; a stone and a key are irregular and need the displacement method.

questions.topic: Volume of Regular and Irregular Solids
questions.question: A student records in Table 9.2: initial 50 mL, final 55 mL, but writes the object's volume as 55 cm³. What is the error?
options: mL readings cannot be converted into cm³ for solids
The initial volume was not subtracted from the final
The object's volume should have been written as 50 cm³
The final reading should have been doubled, not copied
questions.explanation: Volume of the object = (B − A) = 55 − 50 = 5 cm³; the student copied the final reading instead of the difference.

questions.question: Generally, how does the density of a substance change when it is heated?
questions.explanation: Density generally decreases with heating and increases with cooling.

questions.question: Why does heating usually lower a substance's density?
options: Particles are destroyed, so mass falls while volume stays the same
Particles come closer, so volume falls while mass stays the same
Particles gain mass, so mass rises while volume stays the same
Particles spread out, so volume rises while mass stays the same
questions.explanation: On heating, particles tend to move apart, increasing the volume; mass does not change. Since density = mass/volume, a larger volume means a lower density.

questions.question: Why does a hot air balloon rise?
options: Hot air inside is less dense than the cooler air around it
Hot air inside is denser than the cooler air around it
Heating adds mass to the air inside the balloon
The hot air dissolves into the surrounding cool air
questions.explanation: Hot air moves up because it is less dense than the cool air around it — the principle the balloon works on.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: generally, the density ______ with increase in temperature.
questions.explanation: Exercise 2(iii): density generally decreases as temperature increases because volume expands while mass is constant.

questions.question: A test tube of water fitted with a glass tube (Fig. 9.26) is placed in hot water at about 70 °C and the level in the glass tube rises. How is the water's density affected?
options: It increases — the water gained mass from the hot bath
It is unchanged — only the level moved, not the volume
It decreases — volume increased while mass stayed the same
It increases — the water became more compact on heating
questions.explanation: Exercise 12: the rising level shows the water expanded (greater volume) with no change in mass, so density = mass/volume fell.

questions.question: If the same test tube set-up (Fig. 9.26) were instead placed in ice-cold water, what would you expect?
options: The level rises and the water's density increases
The level falls and the water's density decreases
The level stays put because cooling has no effect
The level falls and the water's density increases
questions.explanation: Cooling makes particles come closer, volume decreases, so the level drops; with the same mass in a smaller volume, density increases.

questions.question: In the Fig. 9.26 experiment, which quantity is kept the SAME and which one CHANGES?
options: Mass stays the same; volume changes
Volume stays the same; mass changes
Both mass and volume stay the same
questions.explanation: No water is added or removed, so mass is constant; heating expands the water, so volume changes — hence the density change.

questions.question: Cooling a substance generally increases its density.
questions.explanation: Density increases with cooling because particles come closer, reducing the volume while the mass stays constant.

questions.question: When a substance is heated, both its mass and its volume increase, so its density stays the same.
questions.explanation: Only the VOLUME increases on heating; the mass does not change, so the density decreases.

questions.question: A metal block is heated. Which of these happen?
questions.explanation: Heating spreads the particles out (volume up) but does not change the amount of matter (mass same); density therefore decreases.

questions.question: Which statement is NOT correct about the effect of temperature on density?
options: Heating increases the volume of a substance
Heating increases the mass of a substance
Heating generally decreases the density of a substance
Cooling generally increases the density of a substance
questions.explanation: Mass does not change on heating — only the volume does. The other three statements are correct.

questions.question: How does increasing pressure affect a gas?
options: Particles move apart, volume increases, density decreases
Particles stay put, volume is unchanged, density is unchanged
Particles move closer, volume decreases, density decreases
Particles move closer, volume decreases, density increases
questions.explanation: For gases, pressure pushes the particles together: smaller volume, same mass, higher density.

questions.question: Why does pressure have only a small effect on the density of liquids?
options: Liquids have no particles to push together
Liquids lose mass when they are compressed
Liquids expand when pressure is applied
questions.explanation: Liquids are nearly incompressible, so pressure barely changes their volume and hence their density.

questions.question: Arrange the three states of matter from MOST to LEAST affected by pressure (as regards density).
questions.explanation: Gases are strongly affected, liquids only slightly (nearly incompressible), and solids even less than liquids — their density change is usually negligible.

questions.question: At what temperature does water have its HIGHEST density?
questions.explanation: Water's density is highest at 4 °C; as it cools further and freezes at 0 °C it expands, so ice is less dense.

questions.question: Why does ice float on water?
options: On freezing, water expands, so ice is less dense than liquid water
On freezing, water contracts, so ice is denser than liquid water
Ice has less mass than the same volume of water because it loses water
Dissolved air bubbles trapped in all ice make it buoyant
questions.explanation: At 0 °C the particles arrange in a way that takes up more space (expansion); the same mass in a larger volume means lower density, so ice floats.

questions.question: Why is the floating of ice important for animals in cold lakes?
options: The ice sinks and warms up the bottom of the lake
The ice layer on top keeps the water below warm enough
Fish can breathe the air trapped inside the ice
The ice dissolves oxygen into the water below it
questions.explanation: Because ice floats, it forms a layer on top, keeping the water underneath warm enough for fish and other creatures even in extreme cold.

questions.question: Which statement about water and ice is NOT correct?
options: Water expands when it turns into ice
Ice is denser than liquid water
Floating ice insulates the water beneath
questions.explanation: Ice is LESS dense than liquid water — that is why it floats. The other statements are from the chapter.

questions.question: Which layer of the Earth is the lightest (least dense)?
questions.explanation: The outermost layer, the crust, is the lightest; density increases as we move towards the centre.

questions.question: How do pressure and temperature change as one moves deeper into the Earth, and what is the effect on materials?
options: Both rise, making materials heavier and more compact
Both fall, making materials lighter and looser
Pressure rises but temperature falls, making materials expand
Both stay constant, so density is the same in all layers
questions.explanation: Going deeper, both pressure and temperature rise significantly, making the materials heavier and more compact — denser layers towards the centre.

questions.question: Which of these are named as layers of the Earth in the chapter?
questions.explanation: The chapter lists crust, upper mantle, lower mantle, outer core and inner core. The ozone layer and troposphere belong to the atmosphere.

questions.question: Water has its highest density at 0 °C, which is why ice forms at that temperature.
questions.explanation: Water is densest at 4 °C. At 0 °C it turns into ice, which is LESS dense because it expands.

questions.question: Increasing the pressure on a gas increases its density.
questions.explanation: Pressure pushes gas particles closer together; volume falls while mass stays constant, so density rises.

questions.question: Asima Chatterjee is renowned for developing which kinds of drugs?
questions.explanation: The 'Be a scientist' box says she is renowned for developing anti-epileptic and anti-malarial drugs.

questions.question: Asima Chatterjee was the ______ Indian woman to earn a Doctorate of Science.
questions.explanation: She became the second Indian woman to earn a DSc, after Janaki Ammal.

questions.question: In which field did Asima Chatterjee become the first woman to receive the Shanti Swarup Bhatnagar Award?
questions.explanation: She was the first woman to receive the Shanti Swarup Bhatnagar Award in chemical science and was also honoured with the Padma Bhushan.

questions.question: How did Asima Chatterjee use solvents and solutions in her work?
options: To make the plants grow faster in the laboratory
To extract and isolate compounds from medicinal plants
To dilute finished drugs before selling them
To measure the density of medicinal plant leaves
questions.explanation: She used solvents and solutions extensively to extract and isolate important compounds from medicinal plants.

questions.question: Which solvent has primarily been used for medicinal formulations in Ayurveda, Siddha and other Indian systems?
questions.explanation: Water has primarily been used; oils, ghee, milk and hydro-alcoholic extracts are also mentioned as solvents.

questions.question: Which substances does the chapter list as solvents used for drug formulations in Indian systems of medicine?
questions.explanation: The chapter names water, hydro-alcoholic extracts, oils, ghee and milk. Petrol, mercury and vinegar are not listed.

questions.question: Where is Ningel, the village where salt is still made by traditional methods?
questions.explanation: Ningel village is in Manipur's Thoubal district.

questions.question: At Ningel, salt solution from wells is boiled in metal pans until salt crystals form. Which chapter idea does this illustrate?
options: Removing the solvent by evaporation leaves the solute behind
Heating a gas solution makes the gas more soluble
Boiling makes the salt denser so it sinks and is collected
Salt is the solvent and water is the solute in brine
questions.explanation: The salty water is a solution (salt = solute, water = solvent). Boiling evaporates the water, so the solution becomes more concentrated until salt crystals separate out.

questions.question: Asima Chatterjee was the first Indian woman to earn a Doctorate of Science.
questions.explanation: She was the SECOND Indian woman to do so, after Janaki Ammal; she was the first woman to win the Bhatnagar Award in chemical science.

questions.question: At Ningel, the finished salt cakes are wrapped in a traditional cloth called a phanek.
questions.explanation: The heritage box says the salt cakes are wrapped in a traditional cloth (phanek) to protect them.
